title: Shoulder dislocation, Bankart and Hill-Sachs lesions
text:
The shallow glenoid trades stability for mobility, making this the most commonly dislocated major joint. Over 95% dislocate anteriorly (abduction and external rotation) through the weak inferior capsule; the humeral head sits below the coracoid, the shoulder looks 'squared off' and axillary nerve function must be tested.
The dislocating head tears the anteroinferior labrum and inferior glenohumeral ligament from the glenoid (Bankart lesion) and impacts on the glenoid rim, creating a posterolateral head defect (Hill-Sachs lesion); both predispose to recurrence, especially in young athletes.
Posterior dislocation follows seizures and electric shocks (the 'light bulb' sign) and is often missed. Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder, associated with diabetes) contracts the capsule and restricts external rotation.

title: Hip dislocation, dysplasia and impingement
text:
Posterior dislocation (knee hits the dashboard with the hip flexed) leaves the leg shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated, and risks sciatic nerve injury and femoral head avascular necrosis; reduction is urgent.
Developmental dysplasia of the hip (breech, first-born girls, family history) is screened by the Barlow and Ortolani manoeuvres; untreated, it leads to a limp and early arthritis.
Femoroacetabular impingement (cam deformity of the head-neck junction or pincer over-coverage by the acetabulum) tears the labrum and causes groin pain on flexion with internal rotation.

title: Knee effusions: haemarthrosis versus septic arthritis
text:
Rapid swelling within hours after injury implies haemarthrosis (ACL rupture, osteochondral or intra-articular fracture, patellar dislocation); swelling over a day suggests a meniscal tear. Fat globules in aspirate indicate fracture.
A hot, swollen knee with fever needs aspiration to exclude septic arthritis (Staphylococcus aureus; Neisseria gonorrhoeae in young adults), which destroys cartilage within days. Gout and pseudogout (negatively vs positively birefringent crystals) are the main mimics. Prepatellar bursitis ('housemaid's knee') is superficial to the patella and does not restrict joint motion.

title: Pulled elbow, elbow dislocation and olecranon bursitis
text:
Pulled elbow (nursemaid's elbow): a sudden pull on a toddler's arm slips the radial head out from the annular ligament; the child holds the arm pronated and refuses to use it, and supination-flexion reduces it.
Posterior elbow dislocation in adults can injure the brachial artery and median or ulnar nerves; the 'terrible triad' combines dislocation with radial head and coronoid fractures.
The olecranon bursa swells with repeated leaning (student's elbow), gout or infection.

title: Rib fractures, flail chest and thoracic outlet syndrome
text:
Middle ribs (5 to 9) fracture most often. Segmental fractures of three or more adjacent ribs create a flail segment that moves paradoxically inward on inspiration, usually with underlying pulmonary contusion. Lower rib fractures (9 to 11) should raise suspicion of liver or splenic injury; first rib fractures signify great force and possible subclavian vessel or brachial plexus injury.
A cervical rib or tight scalene triangle compresses the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and subclavian artery or vein (thoracic outlet syndrome): ulnar-sided paraesthesia, hand wasting, Raynaud-like symptoms or effort thrombosis of the subclavian vein (Paget-Schroetter syndrome).

title: Intercostal nerve blocks and herpes zoster
text:
The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove along the inferior border of each rib in the order vein, artery, nerve (VAN), so needles and chest drains are placed just above the rib below. Intercostal nerve blocks relieve pain from rib fractures and thoracotomy.
Reactivated varicella-zoster virus in a dorsal root ganglion causes a painful, band-like dermatomal vesicular rash (shingles), most often in a thoracic dermatome, which does not cross the midline; post-herpetic neuralgia can persist for months.

title: Inguinal and femoral hernias
text:
Indirect inguinal hernias pass through the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, along a patent processus vaginalis, and can descend into the scrotum; they are the commonest hernia in both sexes and in children. Direct hernias push through the weak posterior wall medial to the inferior epigastric vessels (Hesselbach triangle) in older men.
Femoral hernias pass below the inguinal ligament through the femoral canal, lateral to the pubic tubercle; the narrow, rigid neck makes strangulation common, so they are repaired urgently. An aberrant obturator artery (corona mortis) crossing the femoral ring can bleed during repair.
The ilio-inguinal and genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve can be entrapped in mesh, causing chronic groin pain.

title: Umbilical anomalies, rectus sheath haematoma and diastasis
text:
Congenital: omphalocele (herniated gut covered by peritoneum and amnion, associated with chromosomal anomalies) versus gastroschisis (uncovered bowel lateral to the umbilicus). A patent urachus leaks urine from the umbilicus; a patent vitelline duct leaks faeces. Umbilical hernias in infants usually close spontaneously.
Rupture of the inferior epigastric artery in the rectus sheath (anticoagulation, coughing) produces a painful, non-mobile mass that persists when the rectus is tensed (Fothergill sign). Diastasis recti, separation of the recti along the linea alba after pregnancy, causes a midline bulge without true hernia risk. Caput medusae radiates from the umbilicus in portal hypertension.

title: Psoas abscess and the psoas sign
text: The psoas lies in a fascial sheath extending from the thoracic spine to the lesser trochanter, so pus from vertebral tuberculosis (Pott disease), Crohn disease, appendicitis, diverticulitis or renal infection tracks down to present as a groin or thigh mass with a hip held in flexion. Extending the hip stretches an inflamed psoas and causes pain (the psoas sign of retrocaecal appendicitis). A psoas haematoma in anticoagulated patients compresses the femoral nerve.

title: Piriformis syndrome
text: In some people the sciatic nerve, or its common fibular division, passes through or above piriformis rather than below it. Spasm or hypertrophy of the muscle compresses the nerve, causing buttock pain and sciatica aggravated by sitting and by passive internal rotation of the flexed hip, without the imaging findings of disc disease. It remains a diagnosis of exclusion.

title: Intramuscular injections into deltoid
text: Deltoid injections are given into the thickest part, about 2.5 to 5 cm below the acromion. Injecting too low risks the radial nerve in the spiral groove; injecting too high into the subacromial bursa causes shoulder injury related to vaccine administration (SIRVA) with bursitis and restricted movement. The axillary nerve runs horizontally around the surgical neck about 5 to 7 cm below the acromion, limiting how far distal a lateral deltoid-splitting incision can go.

title: Latissimus dorsi flap
text: Because of its large size and single dominant vascular pedicle (the thoracodorsal artery), latissimus dorsi is a workhorse flap for breast reconstruction and covering chest wall defects, and can even be wrapped around the failing heart (cardiomyoplasty). Loss of the muscle is well tolerated. The thoracodorsal nerve can be injured during axillary node dissection, weakening extension and internal rotation.

title: Pelvic ring disruption and osteitis pubis
text:
The pelvic ring rarely breaks in only one place. An anteroposterior compression ('open book') injury separates the symphysis and opens the sacroiliac joints, tearing the pelvic venous plexuses and causing life-threatening haemorrhage; a pelvic binder closes the ring. Associated injuries include urethral rupture at the membranous urethra (blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate) and bladder rupture.
Osteitis pubis causes pubic pain in kicking athletes. Symphysis pubis dysfunction occurs in pregnancy as relaxin loosens the joint.

title: Coccydynia and pilonidal disease
text: Pain at the coccyx after a fall or childbirth is aggravated by sitting and rising from sitting. Pilonidal sinuses in the natal cleft over the coccyx arise from hairs driven into the skin, forming recurrent abscesses in hirsute young men. Sacrococcygeal teratoma is the commonest neonatal tumour.

title: Mesenteric ischaemia and watershed areas
text:
Acute mesenteric ischaemia (atrial fibrillation embolus lodging just beyond the origin of the superior mesenteric artery, where it leaves the aorta at an acute angle) causes severe pain out of proportion to examination findings, lactic acidosis and bowel infarction.
Chronic mesenteric ischaemia causes post-prandial 'intestinal angina', food fear and weight loss. Ischaemic colitis favours the watershed zones at the splenic flexure (Griffiths point, between SMA and IMA territories) and rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck point).
Median arcuate ligament syndrome compresses the coeliac trunk.

title: Portal vein thrombosis and portosystemic anastomoses
text:
The portal vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas by union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. Portal hypertension (cirrhosis most often; portal vein thrombosis; schistosomiasis) opens anastomoses with systemic veins: oesophageal (left gastric to azygos: varices), rectal (superior to middle/inferior rectal: rectal varices), paraumbilical (to epigastric veins: caput medusae) and retroperitoneal.
A transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) decompresses the portal system but can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy. Pylephlebitis (septic portal thrombosis) can follow appendicitis or diverticulitis, causing liver abscesses.

title: Splenic artery aneurysm and ulcer haemorrhage
text:
The tortuous splenic artery is the commonest site of visceral artery aneurysm, more frequent in women and at particular risk of rupture in pregnancy. Posterior penetrating ulcers and pancreatitis can erode the splenic artery, forming pseudoaneurysms.
The gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum; erosion by a posterior duodenal ulcer is the classic cause of massive upper GI bleeding needing endoscopic or surgical control.

title: Renal artery stenosis
text:
Reduced renal perfusion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, causing resistant hypertension, flash pulmonary oedema and a rise in creatinine after starting ACE inhibitors. Atherosclerosis affects the ostium in older patients; fibromuscular dysplasia gives a 'string of beads' appearance in the mid to distal artery of young women. Renal arteries are end arteries, so emboli cause wedge-shaped infarcts.
The left renal vein passes between the aorta and SMA and can be compressed there (nutcracker syndrome), causing haematuria and a left varicocele.

title: Ureteric injury and obstruction
text:
The ureter is at risk in pelvic surgery where it passes under the uterine artery or ductus deferens ('water under the bridge'), at the pelvic brim near the ovarian vessels, and during colorectal surgery. Stones lodge at the pelviureteric junction, the crossing of the iliac vessels and the vesicoureteric junction.
Pelviureteric junction obstruction (often a crossing lower pole vessel) causes intermittent loin pain after drinking large volumes. Retroperitoneal fibrosis draws the ureters medially and obstructs them. A duplex ureter from the upper pole typically inserts ectopically below the normal orifice and may obstruct (ureterocele).

title: Urethral injury, stricture and hypospadias
text:
Pelvic fractures shear the membranous urethra at the urogenital diaphragm (blood at the meatus, high-riding prostate; do not catheterise blindly). Straddle injuries crush the bulbar (spongy) urethra against the pubis, allowing urine to extravasate into the superficial perineal pouch, spreading into the scrotum, penis and anterior abdominal wall beneath Scarpa's fascia but not into the thighs (Colles fascia attaches to the fascia lata).
Gonococcal urethritis and instrumentation cause strictures. Hypospadias, from failed fusion of the urethral folds, opens the urethra on the ventral penis.

title: Pudendal nerve block and entrapment
text:
The pudendal nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament, and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen into Alcock's canal. The ischial spine, palpable per vaginam, is the landmark for pudendal nerve block in the second stage of labour.
Compression in Alcock's canal (cycling, prolonged sitting) causes perineal pain worse when seated and relieved by sitting on a toilet seat. Stretch injury during childbirth contributes to faecal and urinary incontinence.

title: Breast cancer spread and axillary dissection
text:
About three-quarters of breast lymph drains to the axillary nodes, so these are the first site of metastasis; sentinel node biopsy identifies the first draining node. Axillary clearance risks the long thoracic nerve (winged scapula), thoracodorsal nerve (weak latissimus dorsi) and intercostobrachial nerve (numb medial upper arm), and causes lymphoedema of the arm.
Medial breast tumours may also spread to parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes. Lymphatic obstruction produces peau d'orange skin; tethering of suspensory (Cooper) ligaments dimples the skin.

title: Inguinal lymphadenopathy
text:
Superficial inguinal nodes drain the lower limb, skin of the lower abdominal wall below the umbilicus, buttock, perineum, scrotum (but not the testis), penis, lower anal canal below the pectinate line and, in females, the vulva and lower vagina. Enlarged nodes should prompt examination of all these areas: scrotal and penile squamous cell carcinoma, anal carcinoma, melanoma of the leg and sexually transmitted infections (lymphogranuloma venereum, chancroid, syphilis).
Testicular tumours bypass these nodes and drain to the para-aortic nodes.

title: Cervical lymphadenopathy
text:
A persistent hard neck node in an adult over 40 is metastatic squamous cell carcinoma from the upper aerodigestive tract until proven otherwise; the level of the node points to the primary (e.g. nasopharynx to posterior triangle nodes, oral cavity to submandibular nodes).
Virchow's node, in the left supraclavicular fossa near where the thoracic duct ends, enlarges with abdominal malignancy (Troisier sign). Painless rubbery nodes suggest lymphoma; matted, caseating nodes with a cold abscess suggest tuberculous lymphadenitis (scrofula).

title: Tongue carcinoma and lingual thyroid
text:
Squamous cell carcinoma usually arises on the lateral border of the tongue, linked to smoking, alcohol and betel nut; base-of-tongue and tonsillar cancers are increasingly caused by HPV-16 and carry a better prognosis. Tip cancers drain to submental nodes, lateral lesions to submandibular and deep cervical nodes, and posterior third lesions bilaterally, so central and posterior tumours spread to both sides.
A lingual thyroid at the foramen caecum results from failed descent and may be the patient's only thyroid tissue.

title: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma and pharyngeal pouch
text:
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, strongly associated with Epstein-Barr virus and common in southern China, often presents with a neck node or unilateral glue ear from Eustachian tube obstruction, and can invade the skull base causing cranial nerve palsies. Enlarged adenoids in children cause mouth breathing, snoring and otitis media with effusion.
Zenker (pharyngeal pouch) diverticulum herniates through Killian's dehiscence between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor, causing dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis and aspiration.

title: Haemospermia and seminal vesicle cysts
text: The seminal glands produce most of the ejaculate volume (fructose-rich, alkaline). Haemospermia in young men is usually benign and self-limiting; in older men it prompts evaluation for prostate cancer. Seminal vesicle cysts are associated with ipsilateral renal agenesis (Zinner syndrome) because both derive from the mesonephric duct. Prostate cancer invading the seminal vesicles upstages the disease.
